fields.Back: A set of atomic values, with a data type specified (e.g. 10-char string, positive integer). Examples: USA_Phone_Numbers, Employee_Ages, Department IDs.
R(A1, A2, ..., An): a relation name R plus a list of attributes; each attribute Aj is the name of a role played by some domain D in R.
r(R): a set of n-tuples {t1, ..., tm}; each tuple is an ordered list of n values <v1, ..., vn> where each vi is in dom(Ai) or is null.
Attribute: a named column in a relation schema. Tuple: a row of a relation.
Degree: the number of attributes (columns). Cardinality: the number of tuples (rows).

fields.Text: The {{c1::degree}} of a relation is its number of attributes; the {{c2::cardinality}} of a relation is its number of tuples.
The BOOK relation Book(Title, ISBN, Author, YearPub, Pub) with four rows has degree {{c1::5}} and cardinality {{c2::4}}.

fields.Front: BOOK example: what are the domains of YearPublished and ISBN?
fields.Back: YearPublished: integers. ISBN: a letter followed by three digits (e.g. A781).

fields.Front: What is the Cartesian product D1 x D2 for D1 = {2,4}, D2 = {1,3,5}?
What is a (mathematical) relation on D1 x D2?
fields.Back: Any subset of D1 x D2, e.g. R = {(2,5),(4,1)}.

fields.Text: With D1 = {Simpson, Flanders, Smithers}, D2 = {Homer, Ned}, D3 = {40, 30}, the product D1 x D2 x D3 has {{c1::12}} tuples, and a relation is {{c2::any subset}} of them.

fields.Front: Define Cartesian product in the review slide's words.
fields.Back: All POSSIBLE tuples that can be produced with all possible attributes over the whole domain for each attribute.

fields.Front: Give the instructor's plain-language definition of a domain, with her examples.
fields.Back: 'It really is just the data type', possibly limited: all USA phone numbers (every 10-digit combination), employee ages (integers from about 16 to 100), or department IDs following the company's rule.

fields.Front: Can you always list every value in a domain? What is the domain in essence?
fields.Back: No (e.g. the real numbers); the domain is the set of possible values that an attribute can take.

fields.Text: In a tuple t = <v1, ..., vn>, the values are ordered by {{c1::the order of the attributes in the schema}}: v1 is the value of A1, v2 of A2, and any vi may be {{c2::null}}.

fields.Front: What STUDENT relation schema does the instructor give as an example?
What is the difference between big R and little r in the relational terminology?
fields.Back: R is the name of the relation schema (Student, Prof, Patient, Doctor); little r is the actual data, the set of tuples at a moment in time (the relation state).

fields.Front: What is another way the instructor says to think of a tuple?
fields.Back: As an instance of the relation, e.g. a particular student such as Homer Simpson: all the attribute values for one particular thing.

fields.Text: The cardinality of a relation is its {{c1::number of rows}}, which is different from last week's cardinality ratio ({{c2::1:1, 1:N, M:N}}) on an ER relationship.

fields.Front: For D1 = {Simpson, Flanders, Smithers}, D2 = {Homer, Ned}, D3 = {40, 30}: how many rows and attributes can a relation have?
fields.Back: Any subset of the 12 tuples: 3 rows, 5 rows, or even all 12; it always has exactly 3 attributes.

fields.Front: What systematic order does the instructor suggest for listing a Cartesian product?
fields.Back: Fix the first value, then the second, and run through the third: (Simpson, Homer, 40), (Simpson, Homer, 30), (Simpson, Ned, 40), (Simpson, Ned, 30), then Flanders, then Smithers.

fields.Front: Why is the Cartesian product important for relations?
fields.Back: Because a relation over those attributes is a subset of the Cartesian product: each element of the product is one possible tuple, and a table is some of those tuples.
